analysis.one_liner: Shields generic drug makers from patent lawsuits over lower-priced 'skinny label' drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with bipartisan support on December 5, 2025 and has sat in the House Judiciary Committee ever since, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug's patent covers only one of its uses, generic makers can get FDA approval for the other, unpatented uses through what's called a 'skinny label' — carving the patented use out of the label. A court ruling (GlaxoSmithKline v. Teva) left generic makers open to patent lawsuits for even that. This bill writes a legal safe harbor into patent law: seeking a skinny label, marketing the drug under it, and even just telling patients it's the generic equivalent would no longer count as patent infringement. It applies retroactively to conduct before enactment and to lawsuits already pending.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs where only some uses are patented: more generic competition on those uses, typically at much lower prices. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers gain certainty that they can pursue skinny labels without facing infringement suits, including suits over conduct and pending cases today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients buying brand-name drugs and generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a statutory safe harbor so that seeking FDA approval of a skinny label, promoting or commercially marketing the drug under it, and describing it as a generic equivalent are not patent infringement of a method-of-use claim.
Extends the same protection to biosimilars (copies of biologic drugs) approved without the patented conditions of use.
Responds to the GlaxoSmithKline v. Teva ruling, which held that generic manufacturers can sometimes be liable for patent infringement when marketing skinny label generics.
Applies to conduct before enactment and to all proceedings pending as of enactment, so it would also affect lawsuits already underway.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers lose one tool for protecting method-of-use patents: the ability to sue generic makers over skinny-label marketing. That somewhat weakens the financial incentive to run clinical trials proving new uses for older drugs, and generic makers still must carve any patented use out of their labels and promotion.

drawbacks.text: The safe harbor is narrower than some generics makers wanted: promotion and marketing are protected only if they do not reference the condition of use claimed in the patent, so generic makers must still steer clear of the patented use in their advertising.
Weakening method-of-use patent enforcement may reduce brand manufacturers' incentive to invest in clinical trials discovering new uses of existing drugs — a cost honest supporters acknowledge.
The bill applies retroactively to conduct before enactment and to pending litigation, which disrupts lawsuits and business expectations that were settled under prior law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the upside is straightforward: cheaper generic alternatives for drug uses that are not actually patented, with less risk that litigation scares generic makers away from the market. The cost falls on brand-name patent holders and partly on incentives for new-use research; the carve-out requiring that promotion avoid patented uses keeps the protection from swallowing the patent entirely. The retroactive application is the most debatable part, since it reaches back into cases already decided by the pre-existing legal rule.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it; it has not received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Cline (R-VA), joined by Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), introduced the bill on December 5, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill has six cosponsors, evenly split between three Democrats and three Republicans.
The only recorded actions are introduction and the referral to the Judiciary Committee; no further steps appear in the action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off so far: because the bill has not moved, they keep the ability to bring patent infringement suits over skinny-label marketing, and patients continue to face the higher prices that follow when generic competition is deterred.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since December 5, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's backers are evenly bipartisan — three Democratic and three Republican cosponsors behind a Republican sponsor and a Democratic original cosponsor — though no votes have occurred.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to sue generic makers over skinny-label marketing of unpatented uses, which limits how long they can keep cheaper copies off the market for those uses. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against patients who pay brand prices.

A statutory safe harbor lets them enter markets for unpatented uses without fear of infringement suits, including suits over conduct and cases pending today. Their gain is the same thing that lowers prices for patients.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: More skinny-label generics on the market means more lower-cost options to cover and dispense. They benefit as intermediaries when generic competition grows.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the thin early profile common to most House bills: a single-chamber referral and no scheduled action. In the roughly two years left in this Congress, it would need the Judiciary Committee to hold a markup and the House to vote — steps most referred bills never reach — and a companion in the Senate. Without a committee commitment, the realistic expectation is that it stalls.
